subject: Archaeology
title: The Roman Sewer: Cloaca Maxima
description: One-minute skill: The Roman Sewer: Cloaca Maxima.

hook.text: Rome's greatest engineering feat might not be the Colosseum. It might be the sewer built in 600 BCE.

buildup.text: The Cloaca Maxima drained the swampy Forum and channeled waste into the Tiber River through stone tunnels.

discovery.text: At its widest, the tunnel is large enough for a horse and cart. It was big enough to serve a city of one million.

twist.text: The sewer is still part of Rome's drainage system today — 2,600 years old and still functioning.

climax.text: The goddess Cloacina was the patron of the sewer. Romans worshipped their plumbing — literally.

punchline.text: Romans built a sewer, worshipped it, and it outlasted their empire.

quiz.question: What is remarkable about the Cloaca Maxima?
options: It was the first sewer to use ceramic pipes
It is still part of Rome's drainage system after 2,600 years
It was large enough to serve as an underground road during floods

details.summary: The Cloaca Maxima, originally built in the 6th century BCE and expanded over centuries, is one of the world's oldest sewer systems. It drained the Roman Forum and channeled waste into the Tiber River, enabling dense urban living. Parts of this ancient sewer are still in use today.
details.whyItMatters: Sanitation infrastructure is invisible but essential. The Cloaca Maxima made Rome's growth possible by solving the fundamental problem of waste removal in a dense urban environment — a challenge not adequately addressed again for centuries.
takeaways: The Cloaca Maxima dates to the 6th century BCE
It drained the Forum and channeled waste into the Tiber
Parts of this ancient sewer system remain in use today

faq.question: How big is the Cloaca Maxima?
faq.answer: At its largest points, the vaulted stone tunnel is over 3 meters wide and 4 meters tall — large enough to navigate by boat, which Roman inspectors reportedly did. The system extends for several kilometers beneath the old city center with multiple tributary channels.

faq.question: Did all Roman cities have sewers?
faq.answer: Major cities did, though few matched Rome's scale. Many smaller towns used open drainage channels or cesspits. Even Rome's system was primarily designed for stormwater drainage rather than human waste, which was often collected in chamber pots and carried to the sewer or farmland.
